cells.h: Letter, Johan Gottlieb Kolbe to his son, 23 August 1830

National Library of South Africa, MSB 751, the G. A. Kolbe Collection, Special Collections, Cape Town. Four pages from the London tailor to his son at the Cape. The catalogue calls it a letter written on his ordination and it is not — it reports the son being “fully accepted by the [L.M.S.] as one of their Missionaries”, which is the acceptance and not the ordination. Read at full resolution from the supplied PDFs on 20 September 2026. The letter →

rows.held: National Library of South Africa, Cape Town — MSB 751, the G. A. Kolbe Collection, Special Collections. A copy supplied by the library is in this archive's unpublished custody store

cells.h: Dictionary of South African Biography — the entry on George Augustus Kolbe

Typescript by Karel Schoeman, dated February 1992 and headed voorlopige teks (provisional text), supplied by Melanie Geustyn of the NLSA. The DSAB was terminated after Volume V in 1987, five years before this was written, so on the published record this typescript is the only form the entry has ever taken. Nine of its statements agree with documents held here; two are demonstrably wrong. Read and tested →

rows.held: National Library of South Africa — Karel Schoeman's typescript, supplied by the library. A copy is in this archive's unpublished custody store. The published volume this entry was written for may never have appeared

cells.h: Sibree, A Register of Missionaries (LMS, 1923)

James Sibree's register of every London Missionary Society missionary. Found free and complete, and it carries Kolbe's whole mission life in one entry. It also settles a question this archive had left open: Mr Miles was the officer who accepted him, not a messenger carrying somebody else's decision. The entry →

rows.held: Free and complete online, found through archive.org — no deep link is recorded here because none was captured at the time

cells.h: The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, Vol. XIV (1829), pp. 313–318

“SPIRIT OF THE PUBLIC JOURNALS — A SINGULAR LETTER FROM SOUTHERN AFRICA. Communicated by Mr. Hogg, the Ettrick Shepherd.” The story the tailor asked his son to verify in 1830. It is fiction by James Hogg, printed as a settler's letter home — so the tailor's scepticism was right and the son was never expected to confirm it. Read from the Internet Archive, item s1id13414270. The story →

rows.held: Vol. XIV (1829), pp. 313–318 — a printed periodical, read online through archive.org; no deep link was captured

Will of JOHANNA CATHARINA MONTJOY, wife of Petrus Jacobus Booysen. Made eighteen years before her death. Cannot be located on film. Transvaal, Weeskamer
Petrus Jacobus Booijsen — generation six, b. Graaff-Reinet c. 1788
Read Parents named: Gerthardus Lödewikus Booijsen and Magdalena de Beer. Eight children. Nothing to leave. Transcribed →

Anna Catharina Johanna Olivier — b. district Cradock c. 1823

entriesNote: ONE ROW, ONE ID, DERIVED FROM THE ROW'S OWN WORDS. These are the same 46 rows the four tables above are built from — not a second register, which is the thing that would drift. A page that rests on a source names its id, the id has to resolve here or nothing renders, and a build gate counts the ones that do not. THE ID IS NOT A POSITION: it is a slug of the row's first cell, so it travels with the row if a table is reordered, where `read-3` would quietly come to mean a different document.
